Sunday. Ankita, twenty, was oiling Kamla Nani's hair on the balcony when Nani said quietly, "My sister and I stopped speaking in 1987 over a gold chain. I always meant to say sorry first. Then she died. I wish I had opened my mouth." Ankita's hands stopped. The words sat on her chest all evening like a stone.
Thursday. In the hostel Ankita reread a draft she had kept for a month: an email to Professor Rao asking to join his river-survey project. She had been too shy to send it. She thought of Nani's voice. Not a weight, she decided. A warning. Which silence would bother her at seventy?
Two weeks later. She had sent it and got an interview. That evening she phoned Nani. "You made me brave." Nani laughed. "Good. Someone should use my mistakes."

qa.q: What did Nani and her sister stop speaking over?
qa.a: They stopped speaking over a gold chain.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel on Sunday after Nani's words, and how had that changed by Thursday?
qa.a: At first the words sat on her chest like a stone; by Thursday she decided they were a warning, not a weight.

qa.q: What choice did Ankita make at the turning point on Thursday?
qa.a: She asked herself which silence would bother her at seventy, and decided to send the email to Professor Rao she had been too shy to send.

qa.q: How might Nani feel hearing 'You made me brave'?
qa.a: She may feel some peace, since her regret has helped Ankita, which is why she laughs and says someone should use her mistakes.

grounding: A young woman hears her grandmother's regret about staying silent, takes it as a warning rather than a burden, and chooses a risk her future self will be glad of.

Sunday night
Tired enough to cancel Nirmala's driving lesson this morning. Didn't. I promised her in March, and she has been practising gear changes on a broom handle. She stalled eleven times, then drove to the gurdwara corner and back, grinning.
Lately I ask myself one question on the metro: when I'm eighty, what do I hope I can say about my life? Not "I had the best appraisal." Something like: I kept my word. I made up with people. My work helped someone.
So this week: drove with Nirmala. Called Bhaji after eight months of silence over the house; we didn't solve it, but we talked for twenty minutes. Said yes to the flood-mapping project at work, though it pays nothing extra.
I still have regrets. I didn't visit Nani enough before she died, and I'll carry that. But I can choose what comes next.
Gurpreet

qa.a: She had been practising on a broom handle.

qa.a: Gurpreet wants to say 'I kept my word, I made up with people, my work helped someone', not just 'I had the best appraisal'.

qa.a: Keeping the driving promise while tired, calling Bhaji after eight months, and taking on the unpaid flood-mapping project.

qa.a: It may show him that Gurpreet values the relationship more than winning the argument, opening a way back after eight months of silence.

grounding: A young professional asks what they want to say at eighty and lets it shape ordinary choices, keeping a promise, repairing a rift and taking meaningful work, while accepting some regrets stay.

Tuesday, late
Spent the afternoon with Dhruv Mama. Every visit it's the same story: the state exam in 1979, the paper that leaked, the cousin who got the post he says was his. Forty-five years, and he still tells it with his fists clenched. Today he added the brother-in-law who never repaid him and the son who "forgot" him.
I didn't correct him or tell him to let go. I just asked what he had wanted to do with that job. He went quiet, then said he'd wanted to build bridges in the hills. For five minutes he wasn't angry, only sad.
On the bus home I felt heavy for him. And I noticed my own jaw was tight about Deshpande taking credit for my report last month. I've told that story four times already.
I don't want to be seventy and still telling the Deshpande story. Stopping at four.
Yogesh

qa.a: He had wanted to build bridges in the hills.

qa.a: Yogesh felt heavy with compassion for Mama, and uneasy on noticing the grudge about Deshpande.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do instead of lecturing Dhruv Mama, and what came of it?
qa.a: Yogesh asked what Mama had wanted to do with the job, and for five minutes the anger turned into sadness that could be shared.

qa.a: He may feel heard for once, which let him show the sadness underneath the anger.

grounding: A new graduate faces many careers and cities with both excitement and dread, caught in comparison until a friend helps him pick a first step.

passage:
The career fair filled the university sports hall with sixty stalls and a noise like a railway station. Akash, twenty-one, had a bag of brochures by eleven: a bank in Mumbai, a solar startup in Pune, a rural fellowship in Odisha, a master's in Germany.
Jahnavi found him on the bleachers. "You look like you've seen a ghost."
"I've seen sixty futures." He laughed, then didn't. "It's exciting. Every stall is a different me. But if I pick solar and the bank was right, I'll spend ten years comparing."
"You already are. You've read the bank brochure four times."
"Because Vivek got the bank, and he posts about it every day."
"Vivek is not you. Circle two you'd be curious to wake up to. Just two."
Akash took out a pen. His hand hovered, then circled solar and Odisha.

qa.q: How many stalls filled the sports hall?
qa.a: Sixty stalls filled the sports hall.

qa.q: What does Akash mean by 'Every stall is a different me'?
qa.a: He feels excited by all the possible selves but also dreads choosing wrongly and comparing forever.

qa.q: What small step did Jahnavi suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Circling just two options he'd be curious to wake up to, which narrows the choice so it doesn't freeze him.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Akash's rereading of the bank brochure?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees it as comparison with Vivek rather than real interest, which is why Jahnavi reminds him that Vivek is not him.

grounding: A graduate at a career fair feels both excitement and dread at many possible futures, stuck comparing until a friend helps narrow the choice.
